title: I built a spearfishing game in Godot entirely with Claude. Here's the sea after 13 passes
author: Panda5Studio
selftext:
Same spot, same camera. Before on top, after on the bottom.

I'm making an underwater spearfishing game in Godot 4, and everything in it was made with AI. Claude Code writes the Godot code and shaders, and it also builds the models and textures in Blender through Python scripts. Once the gameplay was settled, I spent two days on the water look.

My first attempts went nowhere. I'd ask for "more realistic water," Claude would change something, and the scene would drift in a different direction every time. What fixed it was defining the goal before anything else: I gave Claude a target image, reference videos, and a list of keywords to search for. Then I let it run with Claude Code's /loop skill. On each loop it checked the scene against the target, picked what was most off, fixed it, and went again. Thirteen loops later, the fog, the way colors fade with depth, the light shafts, and the seagrass motion had all been reworked one at a time.

The biggest lesson for me: decide what "done" looks like before the first prompt. Once Claude had a clear goal and material to research, the loop kept moving closer instead of drifting.

Curious how others handle this. Has anyone else tried letting the AI iterate on visuals in a loop, or do you still review every pass by hand?

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body: After I did like million shaders for water I can definitely appreciate a nice looking water. But I think me personally would try to push it even further. Caustics are nice, lighting is also nice, but I feels you miss small details that make it look alive, I can see individual fish in distance but maybe fish that swim in groups like a pool of fish should swim around, crabs and other sea creatures, bubbles going from bottom to the top. Just small things that are not interactive but add more “life” and “details” 🤗

replies.author: Panda5Studio
replies.body: Thank you, that means a lot from someone who's written that many water shaders! I put a lot into the water, the ruins, the rocks, and the seaweed, but I never really thought about whether the sea itself feels alive. That's a great point. I'm taking your advice and running the loop again with that in mind.🐠🦀

comments.author: ArtificialImages
comments.body:
Letting ai edit view and tweak visuals can go either way. Sometimes it feels critical, some times it feels like a waste of time. 

It can help the ai understand what you mean when its coupled with a description. And even without one sometimes, a lot of times even, it can pick up on the issues. 

But is it best practice? No. I would say giving the ai all the info you can without overwhelming it is. 

Quality and technology wise this scene is unimpressive. 

As a game dev I already owned bots a decade ago that could build this. I built them myself. Why? Because its incredibly easy. 

Place a plane, add a noise map, make that noise height  displacement and normal.

Add a ground plane, do the same. 

Make shaders. This should be easy. Blue for sea with some spec and opacity. Tan for sand with some random noise from grains. 

Add fog, set it to blue, tweak settings. 

Use point samples to place grass planes. 

So whilst its a fun test and a good start on a little ocean map. Beware that this is not the best use of ai at present and spending money on this would be a massive, massive mistake. 

In total: do not spend money on these scenes they take a beginner a couple hours in ue5. 

Spend money on complex code you cannot do yourself 

Financial advice from a pro game dev and ai fan 

Good luck have fun.

replies.author: Panda5Studio
replies.body: Thanks for the detailed take! You're right that the scene itself is simple, and giving the AI as much info as possible without overwhelming it is a great point. I'll keep that in mind.

comments.author: yaosio
comments.body:
I found that working on one thing at a time is better than trying to make it do a particular effect that you want. The way to do this is to give the goal to the ai, but ask it to work on things one feature at a time. This way at each step you know what it looks like rather than having it spend more time misunderstanding you or getting it wrong completely. 

I'm doing this with a software toy I'm making with Claude. Rather than telling it all of my ideas all at once I give it one idea at a time. As a bonus this lets me see if the idea actually works rather than trying to guess if an idea does or doesn't work on its own or if it's in combination with something else. As a triple bonus I'm getting more ideas as we work on it. Originally it was going to be an incremental game where you fill up a big space with blocks. Claude had this idea for a character that climbs the tower to grab items. Is eventually turned into watching the character climbing being more fun than actually dropping blocks which made it into a software toy rather than a game. I do have all sorts of ideas for the player but the original idea of it being an incremental game is gone.

replies.author: Panda5Studio
replies.body: Thanks for sharing all this, really interesting! Giving the goal up front but building one feature at a time matches what I found too. And I love how your game turned into a toy because you let the ideas grow step by step. Good luck with it!

I love this!
